lab_title: AR Lab: 3D DNA Structure and Semiconservative Replication
top_level_objectives: Interpret the 3D double-helix geometry of DNA (antiparallel sugar-phosphate backbones and inward-projecting bases)
Apply complementary base-pairing rules (A–T with two H bonds; G–C with three) to predict paired bases
Explain how backbone directionality (5'→3' vs 3'→5') leads to continuous leading-strand synthesis and discontinuous lagging-strand synthesis
Describe the semiconservative mechanism of DNA replication and identify which strand(s) are parental vs newly synthesized

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the 3D DNA model and orient students to its major structural features.
key_visuals: A floating double helix with a highlighted central axis
Two spiraling backbones shown in contrasting colors along the outside of the helix
Base pairs indicated as pairs projecting inward from the backbone toward the axis
student_actions: Rotate the DNA model to view the helix from multiple angles
Point out where the sugar-phosphate backbones are located and where the bases project
Identify a short segment of the backbone and locate the direction labels (5' and 3') on each strand

scenes.brief_purpose: Make antiparallel orientation concrete by linking backbone directionality to the helix geometry.
key_visuals: Direction arrows placed along each backbone showing one strand running 5'→3' and the other 3'→5'
A single highlighted ‘cut’ through the helix revealing the two backbones running in opposite directions
A semi-transparent overlay showing the replication-fork region would later form at a particular location along the helix
student_actions: Trace the highlighted 5'→3' direction on one strand and then repeat on the complementary strand
Answer a quick prompt: which backbone direction will constrain new strand synthesis and how (based on later polymerase rules)
Predict where base pairing will be preserved when the strands separate at a fork

scenes.scene_name: Scene 3: Base Types and Complementary Pairing
scenes.brief_purpose: Enable students to associate A, T, G, and C with correct hydrogen bonding and pairing partners in 3D.
key_visuals: Inward-facing bases labeled (A, T, G, C) at multiple rungs across the helix
Hydrogen bonds drawn as colored dotted lines: two bonds for A–T and three for G–C
Paired bases highlighted simultaneously across the two strands to emphasize complementarity
student_actions: Select a base on one strand and determine its partner on the opposite strand using complementary rules
Verify the number of hydrogen bonds for the selected pair by observing the bond visualization
Complete a short pairing exercise: students choose correct pairs for a set of rungs and justify via H-bond counts

scenes.scene_name: Scene 4: From Double Helix to Replication Fork
scenes.brief_purpose: Connect structure to the replication process by visualizing unwinding and stabilization of strands.
key_visuals: A replication fork marker placed on the helix with the double helix beginning to unwind
Helicase indicated at the fork, with the helix twisting open
Single-strand binding proteins shown coating exposed bases on separated strands
student_actions: Observe the unwinding event and describe what happens to the base pairing when strands separate
Track which parental strand each new strand would be built from once polymerization begins
Confirm the role of stabilizers: prevent re-pairing or re-annealing of exposed strands

scenes.scene_name: Scene 5: Leading vs Lagging—Why Synthesis Becomes Asymmetric
scenes.brief_purpose: Demonstrate how polymerase directionality (5'→3') produces continuous leading and discontinuous lagging synthesis.
key_visuals: DNA polymerase highlighted near both sides of the fork with an arrow indicating 5'→3' extension
A continuous ‘leading strand’ growth path following fork movement
A broken/stepped ‘lagging strand’ growth path labeled as Okazaki fragment formation
A schematic overlay mapping time/space along the fork to show discontinuity
student_actions: Determine which parental template is used to create the leading strand based on 5'→3' compatibility
Identify where Okazaki fragments form on the lagging side and why they must be discontinuous
Explain in words how antiparallel architecture forces this asymmetry in synthesis

scenes.brief_purpose: Conclude by having students classify which strands are conserved and which are newly synthesized in the daughter molecules.
key_visuals: Two separated daughter DNA helices forming in the AR space
One strand per daughter helix highlighted as ‘parental’ (original-colored) and the other as ‘newly synthesized’ (new-colored)
Labels indicating semiconservative replication: each daughter contains one old strand and one new strand
student_actions: For each daughter molecule, identify which strand is parental and which is newly synthesized
Confirm that complementary base pairing remains consistent after replication
Answer a final check: why the process is called semiconservative (not conservative or dispersive), using the visualization as evidence
